nameStory: Catchweed bedstraw earned its name from its incredibly clingy nature - the tiny hooks covering its stems and leaves grab onto everything they touch like nature's velcro. It's also called 'sticky willy' and 'cleavers' for the same reason, because it literally cleaves or sticks to your clothes, pet fur, and anything else that brushes against it. The 'bedstraw' part comes from historical use of these plants as mattress stuffing.
description: Catchweed bedstraw is a sprawling annual plant that grows in tangled mats, using its sticky stems to climb over other plants and spread across the ground. It typically reaches 2-4 feet long with weak, square stems covered in tiny backward-pointing hooks. The plant has narrow leaves arranged in whorls of 6-8 around the stem, and produces tiny white flowers in spring. This common weed is part of the madder family, related to coffee plants.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Sprawling, weak-stemmed plant that forms tangled mats and climbs over other vegetation using tiny hooks - you'll feel it grab your clothes as you walk through it

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged in whorls of 6-8 around the stem, with tiny hooks along the edges that feel rough when you run your finger along them

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers, less than 1/8 inch across, appearing in small clusters from the leaf joints in spring - so small you might miss them at first glance

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square stems covered in backward-pointing hooks that feel scratchy to the touch and make the plant cling to everything - run your hand down the stem to feel the catches

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, round, twin fruits covered in hooked bristles that stick even more tenaciously than the plant itself - nature's ultimate hitchhikers

habitat: Look for catchweed bedstraw in disturbed soils, gardens, waste areas, and along trails and roadsides throughout New England. It thrives in rich, moist soil and partial shade, often forming dense patches in areas where the ground has been disturbed. You'll commonly find it growing up through other plants in gardens, along fence lines, and in forest edges.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge early and begin their rapid sprawling growth, with tiny white flowers appearing from April through June. This is when the plant is most tender and easiest to pull.
seasonality.summer: Plants continue growing and spreading, developing their characteristic clingy mats and producing the hooked seed pods that will stick to everything that passes by.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and disperse by hitchhiking on animals and clothing. The annual plants begin dying back as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems may persist through early winter, but this annual plant dies completely and won't reappear until seeds germinate the following spring.

funFact: Catchweed bedstraw is completely edible and has been used as food for thousands of years - the young leaves can be cooked like spinach, and the seeds can be roasted and ground as a coffee substitute that actually contains caffeine, since it's related to coffee plants!
confusionNotes: Catchweed bedstraw might be confused with other bedstraws, but it's the only one that grabs you so aggressively - if it doesn't stick to your clothes when you touch it, it's probably a different bedstraw species. Remember: if it's not clingy, it's not catchweed!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being considered a garden weed by many, catchweed bedstraw is actually a valuable early-season food source for wildlife and has a long history of human use for food, medicine, and even as a natural strainer for milk. The hooks that make it so annoying are actually an ingenious evolutionary adaptation for seed dispersal.
compareHints: Among New England's bedstraws, catchweed is unique for its extremely clingy nature and annual growth habit. Other bedstraws like Northern Bedstraw or Sweet Woodruff have similar whorled leaves but lack the aggressive hooks and don't grab onto clothing. Hedge Bedstraw is perennial and much less sticky, while Lady's Bedstraw has yellow flowers instead of white.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Hedge bedstraw differs from other common bedstraws by its smooth stems and purely white flowers - catchweed bedstraw has sticky stems, lady's bedstraw has yellow flowers, and fragrant bedstraw has a sweet vanilla scent when crushed.
Unlike its weedy cousin catchweed bedstraw which grabs onto your clothes with hooked bristles, sweet woodruff stays put and feels soft to touch.
Among New England's bedstraws, fragrant bedstraw is unique for its sweet vanilla scent when crushed – most other bedstraws are odorless or have different scents.
Among New England's 15+ bedstraw species, licorice bedstraw stands out with its consistently four broad, oval leaves per whorl - most others have 6-8 narrow, linear leaves arranged in circles.
Marsh-bedstraw is distinguished from other bedstraws by its preference for consistently wet habitats and its delicate, mat-forming growth pattern.
Lady's bedstraw stands out among New England's bedstraws because of its bright yellow flowers - most other bedstraw species have white or greenish blooms.
Among New England's bedstraws, rough bedstraw is distinguished by its prominent stem hooks and preference for wet areas.
Unlike catchweed bedstraw with its velcro-like sticky stems or sweet woodruff's hay-like fragrance, Torrey's wild licorice has smooth stems and that distinctive taste.
Unlike catchweed bedstraw which has sticky, grabby stems and four-petaled flowers, three-petal bedstraw feels smoother and has its distinctive three-petaled blooms.
Among the 15+ bedstraw species in New England, stiff marsh bedstraw is one of only two with 3-petaled flowers (the other being three-petal bedstraw).
Among New England's bedstraws, hairy bedstraw is unique for its consistently soft, fuzzy texture throughout the plant.

White bedstraw differs from other New England bedstraws by its upright growth habit and smooth stems - catchweed bedstraw has hooked bristles that grab onto clothing, while lady's bedstraw has bright yellow flowers instead of white.
Unlike the common catchweed bedstraw with its grabby, rough stems, boreal bedstraw is soft and non-sticky.
Northern bedstraw differs from other New England bedstraws by its upright growth habit and narrow leaves with three parallel veins.
Among New England's bedstraws, bluntleaf bedstraw stands out for its preference for wet habitats and those distinctive rounded leaf tips.
